items.title: Climate heat disasters fuel the health and care workforce crisis: a comparative assessment of workforce heat-health policy in selected European countries
items.abstract: Abstract Background. A majority of European countries have heat-health action plans in place or under development, yet the health and social sectors are poorly considered despite their high burden and key role for health system resilience and security. Objectives. This research connects workforce policy and heat-health action policy, aiming to assess preparedness, protection and agency of health and care workers and identify gaps and capacities for implementation. Methods. Qualitative comparative methodology and a country case study design were applied and a rapid assessment of eight European countries performed during August/September 2026. A semi-structed topic guide informed data collection, drawing on policy documents and other secondary sources. Results. No country case study established a dedicated workforce-centred heat-health strategy nor do they have routine workforce-specific heat-health surveillance systems in place. Countries recognise health workers primarily as service providers, rather than as a workforce requiring protection. This approach shapes all areas of heat-health action. Preparedness of health workers shows limited strategic action but with some adaptations at the provider and individual level and in the education sector. Protection remains poorly addressed and equality, gender equality and migrant health workers are largely absent. Professional stakeholders and bottom-up emerging adaptations create capacities but agency is limited. Four interrelated priorities for advancing workforce heat-health policy can be identified: alignment of heat-health policy and occupational health law; workforce-specific surveillance and monitoring; stakeholder involvement and transsectoral governance; and a European Union strategy. Conclusions. Workforce resilience and climate-health resilience must be addressed together to ensure health security.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: Cognitive Load in Generative AI-Supported Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but how GenAI-supported interaction relates to students’ cognitive load-related experiences remains unclear. This review examined empirical studies published between 2022 and 8 May 2026 that investigated higher education students’ interaction with GenAI systems and cognitive load-related experiences. Twenty-one studies met the inclusion criteria, covering diverse learning contexts including language and writing, STEM, professional education, design, and self-regulated learning. Across studies, findings revealed diverse cognitive patterns rather than a consistent cognitive outcome of GenAI-supported learning. Some studies suggested that GenAI was associated with reduced unnecessary cognitive demands through explanation, feedback, and support. The findings suggest that reduced cognitive demand may reflect effective cognitive support, while some cases may indicate possible cognitive offloading when learners do not actively engage with AI-generated information. Overall, GenAI may provide greater learning value when interaction design reduces unnecessary difficulty while maintaining learners’ active engagement in evaluation and reflection.

items.title: Counteracting threat bias: A longitudinal field experiment testing two interventions that expand managerial attention to opportunities under economic threat.
items.abstract: When economic threat is salient, managers focus on preventing losses and neglect the opportunities adaptation requires, a pattern termed threat bias. On the prevailing view, managerial attention is limited so that attention to threat comes at the expense of attention to opportunity: Restoring it means perceiving less threat or relaxing vigilance, and the remedy has been to divide the orientations across people or units. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, in which promotion and prevention are independent systems, I propose instead that threat bias reflects a situational construal: Salient threat makes prevention cues dominant, while promotion cues lie dormant, so their relation is not fixed. I test this with two brief construal-shaping interventions, one highlighting opportunities (opportunity) and one highlighting opportunities and threats (balanced), in a five-wave field experiment with 414 managers during the COVID-19 downturn, with voice rated by higher level managers blind to condition. Among unexposed managers, within-person increases in perceived threat were associated with lower promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, the threat-bias pattern. Both interventions weakened that association and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice relative to control, under sustained economic threat. The balanced intervention also increased prevention focus and threat-related voice; the opportunity intervention changed neither. Mean perceived threat was unchanged: The interventions altered how managers responded to threat, not how much threat they perceived. Intervention effects on voice grew over 3 months. Threat bias therefore reflects how managers construe the situation rather than an unavoidable trade-off between the orientations, and both can be raised in the same managers at once. items.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption
items.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

items.title: Discretization or Sequentiality? Exploring UI Layouts for Reading-to-Learn Processes on Mixed Reality Headsets
items.abstract: As mixed reality (MR) systems grow in popularity, understanding how virtual-physical panel layouts impact reading and learning is crucial. This study investigates four MR layout designs driven by two dimensions: discretization (continuous vs. discrete) and sequentiality (progressive vs. full disclosure). We conducted two experiments: a 24-participant study using low-difficulty reading materials to gather user perspectives, and a 48-participant study evaluating learning performance and user experience (UX) during high-difficulty tasks. Results indicate that continuous, full-disclosure layouts reduced reading time and improved UX by lowering motion sickness and workload compared to discrete, full-disclosure designs. Conversely, discrete, progressive-disclosure layouts required more time but yielded higher knowledge acquisition than other patterns. These findings provide actionable insights for MR designers creating interfaces that integrate virtual information with physical reading materials to optimize both user comfort and learning outcomes.

items.title: Effects of Gaze Point and Trajectory Factors on Gaze Gesture Interaction Performance in a Simulated Reading-Interface Page-Turning Task
items.abstract: Gaze-gesture interaction offers an alternative to conventional gaze selection, yet the combined effects of interface parameters remain underexplored. This study examined how gaze point size, position, trajectory length, and direction affect accuracy (ACC) and response time (RT) in a simulated page-turning task involving 35 participants. Results showed that larger gaze points and fixed positioning improved ACC and reduced RT. Shorter trajectories reduced RT without significantly affecting ACC, while horizontal trajectories improved ACC compared with vertical trajectories, with no significant RT difference. Significant interactions in ACC indicated that the effects of gaze point size and trajectory direction depended on positioning conditions. Under free positioning, accuracy gains plateaued beyond 128 px, whereas fixed positioning maintained improvements with increasing size. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of jointly optimizing gaze-gesture parameters and suggest that larger gaze points, fixed positioning, shorter trajectories, and horizontal movements offer favorable performance within the tested conditions.

items.title: Evaluating AI Alignment in LLMs: Output Analysis of Value Priorities Across 75 Models with Human Benchmarking
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) shape human–AI interaction, yet capability and safety benchmarks provide limited insight into their expressed value priorities. Across three studies, we developed an output-based approach to evaluating correspondence between LLM priorities and human judgements of optimal AI functioning. Study 1 identified six themes through inductive qualitative analysis: Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 found stable rankings within models and a shared priority structure across models. Study 3 compared 75 LLMs with 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric combining profile shape and calibration of between-priority differences. Many models reproduced the human profile while exaggerating differences between priorities. Fidelity varied across models, with no clear pattern linking fidelity to more recent releases. Both humans and LLMs assigned Agency low priority. This framework offers a standardized method for auditing expressed value profiles across models alongside capability, safety, and output evaluations.

items.title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
items.abstract: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

items.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
items.abstract: Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

items.title: From driving (L0) to living (L5): Intergenerational car comfort concept by Etic-emic theory
items.abstract: This study explores intergenerational vehicle comfort using the Etic-Emic framework, translating a psychological concept into automotive guidelines. A scoping review identified 34 parameters, and trend analysis of 1789 Scopus articles (1953-2025) tracing comfort across vehicle generations. Expert interviews with 15 specialists classified them as Etic (relevant to L0 and L5) or Emic (emerging specifically in L5), suggesting additional factors. Group brainstorming refined classifications, yielding 44 parameters, including factors such as brand identity and cargo space. Safety, vibration control, and fuel efficiency were stable Etic parameters, whereas non-driving tasks, confidence to sleep or fully recline, legal liability transparency, and cybersecurity were Emic. The novel "Intergenerational Car Comfort" concept provides OEMs an actionable decision tool: its Etic-Emic matrix guides trade-offs, including safety constraints versus expectations to recline and sleep. items.title: From isolated countermeasures to organizational practice: A systematic review of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare
items.abstract: Occupational fatigue poses persistent workforce and safety risks in healthcare. Other safety–critical sectors manage fatigue through structured fatigue risk management systems (FRMS), but whether healthcare’s evidence supports similar system-level claims is unclear. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the effects, implementation, and certainty of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare. PubMed, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 1 June 2026. Studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, synthesized narratively per Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guidance, and assessed for implementation and certainty using Proctor’s framework and GRADE. Thirty-four publications representing 32 studies were included across four strategy groups: work-schedule and duty-hour controls; multicomponent programs and education/coaching; nap and restorative-break practices; and digital monitoring and real-time countermeasures. No included study evaluated a complete, formally governed fatigue risk management system; the evidence concerned isolated or bundled workplace strategies. Naps and restorative breaks showed the most recurrent short-term signals for reduced fatigue/sleepiness and improved vigilance or cognitive performance, though findings were inconsistent; evidence for other strategies was weaker, and patient-safety, organizational, and economic outcomes were rarely evaluated. Implementation evidence concentrated on acceptability and fidelity; organizational governance, structured risk assessment, reach, cost, and sustainability were unexamined, and certainty was predominantly low or very low, with one moderate-certainty exception for increased sleep duration under reduced-duty schedules. Healthcare has thus tested individual countermeasures rather than embedded fatigue risk management within organizational practice; advancing the field requires linking local hazards to supported controls, with particular attention to the governance and risk-assessment structures that remain least developed.

items.title: GeoST: Object-Local Representations and Geometric Support-Guided Temporal Fusion for Maritime Ship Detection in Point Clouds
items.abstract: Reliable environmental perception is essential for intelligent ships, with three-dimensional (3D) point cloud ship detection providing spatial information for situational awareness and collision avoidance. However, unstable cross-frame geometric correspondence, ambiguous historical associations, and unreliable temporal fusion hinder the use of historical information. We propose GeoST for temporal maritime LiDAR ship detection, using object-local representations as a basis for geometric support-guided historical feature modulation and fusion. Built on FASTer, GeoST normalizes observations within their respective proposal coordinate systems and associates them by object dimensions and shape, constructing temporal inputs without external ego-vessel poses. The multi-scale anisotropic point feature enhancement module (PointMKDA) aggregates neighborhood features across scales and orientations to enhance local geometric representations. The geometrically constrained cross-attention module (GCAM) uses enhanced current-frame focal point features to update historical features and estimate geometric support. The reliability-guided feature modulation (RGFM) module combines this support, association priors, observation age, and learned features to generate modulation weights across temporal, point, and channel dimensions, regulating feature contributions before temporal fusion. GeoST achieved 3D average precision (AP) of 87.17% and 73.09% at intersection-over-union (IoU) thresholds of 0.5 and 0.7, respectively, exceeding FASTer by 2.81 and 2.27 percentage points.

items.title: Not Interchangeable: Pilot Self-Reports and Instructor Competency Ratings as Cognitive-State Labels in Real Flight Operations
items.abstract: Objective To quantify the correspondence between pilots’ post-task workload and situation-awareness ratings and instructor competency ratings during real flight. Background Adaptive systems, neuroergonomic classifiers, and competency-based training all need cognitive-state labels. Self-reports capture felt demand and awareness; instructor evaluations capture behaviorally inferred competence. Method Forty pilots completed five Cessna 172 tasks during dedicated research flights. After each task, pilots gave single-item 0–10 ratings of workload and situation awareness. One flight instructor at each of the two participating organizations rated Situation Awareness and Workload Management on 1–4 International Civil Aviation Organization-aligned scales, and rated task execution with behavior-specific items, before hearing the self-ratings. Analyses used Spearman correlations with participant-clustered bootstrap intervals, within-person decomposition, and mixed-model and stratified sensitivity analyses. Results Pooled cross-source correspondence was weak for situation awareness ( ρ = . 08 ) and workload ( ρ = − . 14 ; . 14 aligned). The two instructor competencies were strongly intercorrelated ( ρ = . 61 ) and strongly associated with same-instructor task-execution ratings ( ρ = . 69 and . 72 ). A small within-person workload signal ( r = − . 19 ) attenuated after double centering. Point estimates were similar in both strata and after excluding pilots aged 60 or older. Conclusion The two sources provided distinct, non-substitutable labels. Their strong link to same-rater task-execution scores is consistent with execution-referenced judgment, though shared-rater variance cannot be ruled out; self-reports captured pilots’ reported experience. Application Cognitive-state monitoring and training assessment should use multi-source labels and should not treat observation-based competency ratings as direct measures of internal workload or situation awareness.

items.title: Occupational Health Risks: Personal Protective Equipment Utilisation and Exposures Among Healthcare Workers Ho West District, Ghana
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: This study assessed occupational exposures, personal protective equipment (PPE) availability and utilisation, and factors associated with PPE utilisation among healthcare workers (HCWs) in Ho West District, Ghana. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 174 randomly selected HCWs from all 32 health facilities. Data collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire in Kobo Collect were analysed in Stata 17. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression were used, with statistical significance set at p<0.05 and a 95% confidence level. Results: Overall, 79.3% of HCWs reported occupational exposure; 112 (64.4%) reported inadequate PPE availability, while 102 (58.6%) had poor PPE utilisation. Gloves were used by 75.3%, compared with gowns (5.8%) and eye protection (3.5%). Blood/body-fluid splashes were reported by 102 (58.6%) and needle-stick injuries by 73 (42.0%); 51.7% reported that exposures occurred rarely. PPE training was associated with higher odds of appropriate utilisation (AOR=2.75, 95% CI: 1.36–5.56; p=0.005), whereas economising on limited PPE supplies was associated with lower odds (AOR=0.34, 95% CI: 0.17–0.69; p=0.003). Conclusion: HCWs in Ho West District experienced substantial occupational exposure alongside inadequate PPE availability and generally poor utilisation. Regular practical training and a reliable, uninterrupted PPE supply are needed to improve appropriate use and reduce occupational risks.

items.title: Progressive Trajectory-Aware Calibration for Human–AI Handoff in Sales Conversations
items.abstract: AI assistants in sales conversations predict conversion probabilities at each turn, but miscalibrated confidence can undermine human–AI handoff decisions. We propose Progressive Trajectory-Aware Calibration (PTAC), a lightweight post-hoc method that adjusts temperature using conversation progress and observed probability trajectories. PTAC requires fewer than 5,000 parameters. On e-commerce data with independently verified outcomes, PTAC reduced turn-stratified calibration error by over 80% at 14% purchase prevalence and by 9% relative to static scaling at the natural 6% prevalence, matching adaptive scaling. It reduced error by 63–78% on call-center data with model-generated labels and by 13% on synthetic dialogues. PTAC improved handoff error rates at fixed human workloads and reduced misplaced reliance at operational thresholds; trust outcomes were simulated and matched-trust performance was comparable. Causal-progress ablation supported deployment-time improvements on call-center and synthetic data; e-commerce gains depended on non-causal turn position.

items.title: Social movements in the production of healthy, sustainable, and health-promoting territories: a scoping review
items.abstract: Health promotion and surveillance, encompassing environmental and occupational aspects, and grounded in a participatory, territory-based approach, integrate a set of concepts designed to support interventions addressing health issues experienced by populations within their own territories (Oliveira; Machado, 2026). The setting where surveillance and health promotion converge is almost invariably the territory, which serves as a central category for analyzing health-disease-care processes. This is because the territory extends beyond its geographical and material dimensions, incorporating social relations, identities, ways of life, cultural practices, and the processes involved in the production and reproduction of life (Santos, 2005). Understanding health-disease-care processes within a specific territory requires an interdependence between health surveillance, which seeks to identify risks, threats, and vulnerabilities affecting populations, and health promotion, which aims to intervene in the determinants that influence living conditions. These approaches encompass various fields of action, including epidemiology, public health, environmental health, and occupational health. Their combined efforts contribute to the prevention of health issues, the reduction of risks, and the development of responses tailored to the specific needs of these territories (Teixeira, 2002; Oliveira & Machado, 2026). The primary milestone in defining health promotion globally is the Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986), developed at the First International Conference on Health Promotion, which posits an expanded concept of health, one encompassing quality of life. Health is linked to access to culture, leisure, sports, work, employment, income, education, housing, social assistance, and healthy environments, among various other dimensions that serve as determinants for the living and health conditions of populations, communities, and territories (Brazil, 2018). Furthermore, promoting health on a global scale has entailed developing intersectoral and participatory actions that enhance the autonomy of individuals and communities, strengthening their collective capacities and contributing to the transformation of the conditions that generate inequalities (Brazil, 2018). After all, no one falls ill or recovers alone; everyone falls ill and recovers collectively, within a community (Teixeira, 2002; Oliveira; Machado, 2026). This expanded conception highlights that health promotion cannot be understood as the exclusive responsibility of health services and professionals; rather, its realization depends on recognizing the diverse ways of being and existing in the world, constructed within specific territories and shaped by socio-environmental determinants (Breilh, 2006). For instance, communities, grassroots leaders, civil society organizations, social movements, cultural groups, environmental collectives, and other forms of collective action can play fundamental roles in identifying problems, advocating for rights, mobilizing resources, and developing responses to local needs. By integrating scientific and popular knowledge, these initiatives help to broaden social participation and strengthen the capacity of populations to intervene in the processes that affect their health and living conditions. The role of social movements takes on particular significance in this context, as these collectives can link local demands to broader agendas, such as social justice, equity, environmental protection, and the safeguarding of rights, that remain under-explored in the literature. Identifying experiences within this field can inform the formulation of participatory, socially just, and epidemiologically efficient policies, drawing upon the knowledge and practices rooted in specific territories. Accordingly, this article aims to map studies that examine how social movements have fostered health promotion and contributed to the creation of healthy and sustainable territories globally.

items.title: The Roles of Critical Thinking and Cognitive Load in the Association Between Digital and Perceived Argumentative Writing Readiness Among Indonesian High School Students
items.abstract: Abstract Background The increasing emphasis on digital-age competencies in secondary education further supports the notion that students' digital literacy statistically predicts argumentative writing skills. However, it is unclear whether digital literacy directly shapes writing readiness or does so through cognitive mechanisms such as critical thinking and cognitive load, particularly among high school students in Global South countries. Objective This study examines a moderated-mediation model of self-reported argumentative writing readiness, in which critical thinking mediates the relationship between digital literacy and students’ self-reported readiness to write argumentative texts among high school students in Indonesia, while cognitive load is tested as a boundary condition that moderates the strength of the critical thinking to writing readiness relationship. Methods This study applied a cross-sectional survey design with a purposive sample of 513 high school students from 12 districts/cities in South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Data analysis was carried out using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapping, with a significance threshold of 0.05. Results The results showed that digital literacy played a significant role in predicting critical thinking (β = 0.736; p < 0.001), and, in turn, critical thinking significantly predicted argumentative writing readiness (β = 0.656; p < 0.001). The indirect pathway from digital literacy to writing readiness via critical thinking was also significant (β = 0.482; p < 0.001). In contrast, cognitive load did not show a significant relationship with writing readiness (β = − 0.031; p = 0.579), even though it was positively predicted by both digital literacy and critical thinking. Conclusion These findings suggest that critical thinking is the main mechanism that fully mediates the relationship between digital literacy and argumentative writing readiness, and interestingly, this mechanism actually strengthens, not weakens, when the cognitive load is at a higher level. weakens, when the cognitive load is at a higher level. Implicitly, digital skill training alone is not enough to improve students’ writing readiness, unless accompanied by explicit critical thinking instruction. On the other hand, cognitively demanding writing tasks do not always need to be minimized, as long as students have critical thinking skills that let them turn that cognitive engagement into productive reasoning.

items.title: From Dialogue to Task: How Cognitive Engagement With Generative Artificial Intelligence Relates to Post-Dialogue Activity and Task Outcomes
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.

items.title: Just AI Governance and the Forbidden-Boundary Principle
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes consequential decisions, yet predictive accuracy is not a sufficient justification for delegated authority. This conceptual study develops an integrated framework for assessing just AI across normative, data, model, and governance layers. Drawing on plural theories of justice, sociotechnical fairness research, and publicly available governance standards, it maps six justice requirements to observable evidence, decision rights, and remedies. It proposes a two-stage evaluation rule: exclude uses that fail independently justified minimum rights constraints, then compare eligible alternatives across multiple performance and governance criteria. As an explicitly limited normative analogy, Genesis chapter 2 motivates a Forbidden-Boundary Principle (FBP), under which an AI agent must not execute externally consequential actions outside pre-authorized boundaries. The resulting First-Principle Safe-Stop Protocol (FPSSP) comprises an independently governed policy monitor, a mandatory execution gate, a restricted or alternative safe-state controller, immutable-oriented audit trails, and accountable human authorization for recovery. We distinguish this normative and traceability contribution from existing Simplex and runtime assurance architectures; we do not claim a novel safety switch or formal proof of universal ethical compliance. A policy schema, threat model, test matrix, outcome definitions, and a prospective comparison design make the proposal falsifiable. No FPSSP implementation, experimental dataset, numerical improvement, or verified latency bound is reported. The framework supports future evaluation rather than constituting evidence of operational safety.

items.title: Repetition bias in self-directed learning
items.abstract: Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into "blocks": they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.

items.title: Design Vulnerabilities and Design Assumptions in Automated Systems: The Case of the B737 MAX Original MCAS Design
items.abstract: In this paper, we demonstrate how formal modeling of human-machine systems can uncover design vulnerabilities. Two fatal accidents involving the Boeing B737 MAX raised substantial safety concerns about the aircraft’s design and led to the worldwide grounding of the MAX. These accidents involved design vulnerabilities, design assumptions about human performance that proved unwarranted, and an operational context that differed from what the designers assumed. The two accidents also involved the operation of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) that was introduced into the pitch trim system of the B737 MAX. We use the case of the MAX to show that by building a formal model of this system including MCAS and examining it with an analytical methodology, the vulnerabilities in the design become visible. By comparing this model with a model of the MAX’s predecessor, the B737NG, we highlight discrepancies between the design assumptions about how pilots would act when faced with system failures and the crew actions observed in the first accident. Using a formal approach to describing human interaction with automated systems to identify design vulnerabilities can be productively employed in the design of automated systems, regulatory assessment, and accident investigation.

items.title: Effects of mini-maps with different reference frames on polarity-free 3D spatial navigation: a behavioural and fNIRS study
items.abstract: Manned spaceflight and deep-sea exploration extend human activities to extreme environments lacking gravitational and visual polarity cues, where spatial disorientation frequently occurs. Mini-map studies largely focus on terrestrial environments, while reference frame design for polarity-free 3D space remains understudied. We constructed a symmetric virtual 3D space in which 31 participants completed four navigation conditions: no map, world-centred static, world-centred dynamic, and egocentric dynamic (EGO) map. Behavioural, subjective and fNIRS data were collected. Results showed significant condition effects on accuracy and reaction time. All three map conditions improved accuracy and reduced right fusiform gyrus deoxyhemoglobin versus no map. The EGO map with trajectory tracking and real-time heading alignment achieved superior accuracy, lower workload and higher usability by lowering path integration demands and reference switching costs. These findings provide support for navigation interface design for spaceflight, deep-sea operations and virtual reality.

items.title: Public perceptions of infrastructural digital nudging: an experience-based study in a quasi-public setting
items.abstract: Abstract Digital nudging increasingly shapes behavior, impressions, and decision-making in public spaces. However, existing empirical research has largely focused on nudging in relation to individualized decision-making, offering limited insight into how diverse publics interpret such technologies when embedded in public infrastructures—what we refer to here as infrastructural digital nudging. In such settings, the influence of digital nudging may become less visible and less easily avoidable, while asymmetries between those who design the technology and those who encounter it may become more consequential. These conditions, together with the possibility that public expectations and social implications extend beyond expert-defined frameworks, highlight the need for early engagement. In this study, we investigate public perceptions of infrastructural digital nudging based on multi-display signage through a demonstration conducted at a national science museum in Japan. We used a convergent mixed-methods design that combined quantitative analyses of structured questionnaire responses with qualitative analyses of open-ended questionnaire responses and sticky notes. This research design enabled both statistical analysis and fine-grained interpretation of participants’ concerns, interests, and imagined uses. Our results show that, at an aggregate level, participants prioritized understanding the technology’s mechanisms, purposes, and social impacts over canonical ethical categories such as autonomy and transparency. However, qualitative analyses revealed considerable heterogeneity: some participants expressed strong concerns about unconscious influence, manipulation, and misuse. Co-occurrence analyses further indicated that participants’ evaluations were structured around different perspectives, including science-focused assessment and social concerns. These findings suggest that public perceptions of infrastructural digital nudging are heterogeneous and organized around multiple perspectives, not reducible to expert-defined categories. This underscores the importance of empirically examining how such technologies are interpreted when encountered in environments approximating real-world situations.

items.title: Too Big to Inspect? Ethically Auditing Large Datasets Through Small Samples
items.abstract: Big techs and researchers increasingly claim that their training datasets are too large to inspect for bias and ethical problems. However, in the race to build ever-large models, they have relied on automated web scraping and no human curation. Datasets built this way absorb the stereotypes, exclusionary norms, and historical prejudices of their sources, and the models trained on them can reproduce and amplify those patterns. Because manually auditing billions of samples is humanly impossible, we need practical, effective methods to identify biases in these datasets. This paper studies the feasibility of ethically auditing large datasets through small samples and proposes a practical method for identifying structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools (AIETs) to random samples. We applied Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels, and Data Cards to a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe. Our results show that evaluating small samples with AIETs can reveal ethical problems, structural biases, and technical inconsistencies. Although industry practice assumes that identifying problems requires analyzing the entire dataset, we show that a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without overwhelming computational or human resources. Demonstrating that a dataset is biased does not require examining every instance: if a bias appears in a random sample, it is a flaw of the creation process. The AIETs' questions acted as provocateurs, evoking different perspectives and analysis methods for the same dataset, but the analysis and its results depended fundamentally on the human factor. We hope these findings contribute to urgent public discussions about ethics, transparency, accountability, and AI regulation by offering a practical pathway for responsibly auditing massive datasets.

items.title: Validation and Evacuee Modeling of Virtual Robot-guided Emergency Evacuation Experiments
items.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is an increasingly common tool for investigating human responses to emergency situations. Nonetheless, studies validating and comparing human subject behavior during real world emergencies to their responses in VR are notably rare, and no prior studies have validated whether human emergency responses to guidance from a robot are comparable in VR versus the real world. In the present pre-registered study, we used VR to replicate a previous robot-guided emergency evacuation study conducted in the real world and compared human subject behavior in matched physical and virtual environments. In both environments, human subjects were asked to follow a robot to a location and to then read an article. While reading, a fire alarm sounds. The robot then attempted to guide them to a distant, unfamiliar exit rather than a nearby and familiar exit. We observed close correspondences between evacuee exit choice (the robot’s distant exit versus closer exits), evacuation time, and self-reported trust in the robot between the VR and physical environments. We further demonstrate that data collected in virtual reality can be used to create accurate motion models (mean positional error of 0.42 meters) predicting evacuee trajectories and locations in the physical environment.

items.title: Who verifies and who continues? Personality and physiological predictors of anomaly-responsive oversight in AI-supported navigation
items.abstract: Intelligent systems increasingly place humans in oversight roles, yet users exposed to the same anomaly warning do not respond uniformly. Across two studies using an AI-supported navigation task, we examined whether warning design, focal HEXACO traits and trial-level physiology explained anomaly-specific evaluation and verification/override behaviour. Both studies used a 2 × 2 manipulation of warning salience and explanation style. Study 1 combined eye tracking and pupillometry; Study 2 used electrodermal activity. Prominent and especially explanatory warnings produced the largest behavioural and evaluative effects. Personality showed smaller effects, with behavioural increments sensitive to model specification; Conscientiousness was most consistently associated with verification, whereas Emotionality was associated with evaluative and physiological responsiveness. Repeated participant-level validation showed substantial incremental prediction from pupil features and smaller gains from electrodermal features, including under temporally restricted sensitivity analyses. The findings support a differentiated person-centred account of anomaly-responsive oversight while separating subjective trust from behavioural reliance and verification.

items.title: A lightweight convolutional neural network for target detection in an edge environment
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.

items.title: A Novel Dual-Function Face-Shield Prototype Integrating an On-Demand Hand-Sanitiser Reservoir: Design and Preliminary Benchtop Evaluation
items.abstract: Background and Objectives: Rapid hand hygiene is difficult to maintain during uninterrupted patient care. We designed and performed a preliminary benchtop evaluation of a proof-of-concept face-shield prototype integrating an on-demand disinfectant reservoir. Materials and Methods: A dual-function wearable system was built from a PETG visor (230 × 230 mm, 0.20 mm) and modular reservoirs (25, 50, 75, 100 mL). Five complete prototype units were fabricated under the same manufacturing conditions: two separate physical units with 100 mL reservoirs (Units A and B) and one unit each with 75, 50, and 25 mL reservoirs. Functional and mechanical testing was performed across the two 100 mL units, with shared and unit-specific endpoints; chemical compatibility was evaluated using dedicated PETG specimens, while ergonomic assessment was limited to biomechanical modelling. Disinfectant density (Mikrozid AF Liquid) was measured (0.875 ± 0.002 g/mL, n = 5) to convert dispensed mass to volume. The valve delivered 3.08 ± 0.21 mL/activation (CV 6.8%, n = 60; 30/unit, single fill, no refilling). Results: The system weighed 103.3 g empty and 190.8 g filled with 100.0 mL of disinfectant (87.5 g disinfectant mass). Recalculated cervical torque (τ = m × g × r; baseline: 0.084 N·m) was 0.118 N·m for the empty-reservoir configuration (+40.6%) and 0.252 N·m for the filled configuration (+199.9%). No continuous leakage occurred (mass loss < 0.1 g), retention exceeded 10 N in all directions, and PETG remained stable after 14-day immersion and 50 wiping cycles. Estimated cost was €10–20/unit. Conclusions: This proof-of-concept supports the technical feasibility of integrating a face-shield platform with immediate access to hand sanitisation in one reusable device, without establishing standards-based protective performance. The small number of separate physical prototypes used for functional testing (two 100 mL units), together with the absence of microbiological, optical-standard and human-factor validation, limits generalisability. Human-participant, microbiological, ergonomic and clinical usability studies are required before clinical implementation. A conceptual touchless valve is proposed for future work.

items.title: Barriers to Social Media Engagement Among People With Dementia: A Qualitative Survey
items.abstract: Social media can offer benefits for people with dementia, including enhanced social connectivity, peer support, and access to information. However, digital exclusion remains an issue, and little is known about factors that deter engagement. This study explored barriers to social media use from the perspectives of people with dementia and their unpaid carers. An online survey was completed by 227 participants (179 carers; 48 people with dementia), including questions about attitudes toward social media. Reflexive thematic analysis of open responses generated six themes: (1) Perceived value of social media; (2) Generational and age-limiting beliefs; (3) Digital access and literacy; (4) Perceived (un)safety of social media; (5) Symptoms of dementia; (6) Heavy caring loads. Social, cognitive, and technological factors perpetuate exclusion from social media among people with dementia. Addressing these barriers requires improved digital access, literacy, and safety, alongside more inclusive platform design and support for carers facilitating engagement.

items.title: Conversational Artificial Intelligence in Community Care: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: The strategic shift toward community-based healthcare, away from hospital settings, is a policy priority internationally. Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) may support this transition, yet its practical applications remain underexplored. This scoping review maps CAI capabilities and their configuration within community care. We searched PubMed, the ACM Digital Library, and selected grey-literature sources for studies published from January 2023 to June 2025. Of 551 records identified, 29 studies were included. We identified 20 capabilities across five functional domains: Understand (n = 5), Transform (n = 3), Remember (n = 3), Generate (n = 5), and Act (n = 4). Findings suggest that CAI extends rather than replaces human care, supporting access, ongoing engagement, and care coordination. Multi-party and expert-in-the-loop designs emerged as recurring implementation strategies. They also surface design tensions, including tradeoffs between reliability and conversational flexibility, and between the benefits of long-term memory and associated privacy risks. The resulting capability-centered taxonomy offers accessible framework for integrating CAI into community care settings.

items.title: CoT4AD: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Explicit Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently attracted growing attention in end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving. While recent works have begun exploring Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to decompose complex driving tasks, they predominantly rely on purely textual reasoning. Driving, however, is an inherently spatial and physical task. Textual-only CoT struggles to capture dynamic geometric changes, frequently leading to numerical hallucinations and unreliable trajectory planning. To bridge the gap between semantic reasoning and the physical action space, we propose CoT4AD, a novel VLA framework that introduces a Hybrid Visual-Language CoT. Grounded in human cognitive Situation Awareness (SA) theory, CoT4AD strictly enforces a causal reasoning sequence: 3D spatial perception, semantic comprehension via Visual Question Answering (VQA), and physical projection via VLM-conditioned future scene diffusion. This hybrid chain explicitly forces the VLM to respect physical laws and spatial constraints before outputting driving trajectories. Furthermore, to balance explicit interpretability with the stringent latency demands of real-world deployment, we introduce an Implicit CoT model via Latent Alignment. This approach distills the multi-step causal knowledge directly into the VLM's hidden states, enabling highly efficient inference without sacrificing reasoning capability. Extensive experiments on both real-world and simulated benchmarks demonstrate that CoT4AD achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, it reaches a leading Driving Score of 81.22 on the Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark and significantly reduces collision rates in nuScenes open-loop evaluations, proving the necessity and effectiveness of physics-grounded visual reasoning in E2E autonomous driving.

items.title: Determining Voice Control Boundaries for in-Vehicle Functions: A User-Engineer-Expert Assessment Framework
items.abstract: Efficiently adapting voice control functions in smart vehicles remains a practical challenge in human-computer interaction. This study established a three-source, lightweight research system comprising user questionnaire survey (N = 326), engineer evaluation from the corporate sector (N = 12), and expert interviews from the industry (N = 8). A six-dimensional weighted adaptability assessment model(SWAAM) was designed (safety risk 30%, operational complexity 20%, usage frequency 15%, command clarity 15%, feedback requirements 10%, and technical feasibility 10%). Within 15 days, a systematic evaluation of 30 vehicle control functions was completed. The results indicate that user voice preference exhibits significant stratification: preference rates for high-frequency comfort functions such as navigation, air conditioning, and media exceed 98%, while preference rates for safety-critical functions such as driver assistance and chassis control are below 60%. Through triangulation validation, 15 items were identified for the whitelist (priority for release), 3 for the blacklist (prohibited from release), and 12 for the graylist (requiring scenario-based release, e.g., window control limited to speeds below 80 km/h, special scenario modes restricted to parking only). Expert consensus established safety red lines and design specifications, including “prohibition of voice control for core driving functions,” “adoption of the “action + object” command format,” and “requirement for secondary confirmation for safety-related functions.” The weighted total score across the six dimensions showed high consistency with the functional list (whitelist ≥ 7 points, blacklist <4.0 points), validating the model’s effectiveness. This method ensures scientific rigor while reducing the adaptation cycle to 15 days. It provides a practical, lightweight framework for rapid iteration in mass-production voice interaction projects.

items.title: Does AI-Generated Content Reduce Cognitive Load? A Comparative Examination of Instructional Materials Using Eye Tracking, Galvanic Skin Response, and Usability Measures
items.abstract: This study compares GenAI-generated, theory-based multimedia, and traditional instructional materials in cognitive load, visual attention, physiological arousal, and perceived usability. Fifty undergraduates evaluated all three conditions in a within-subjects repeated-measures design. Fixation count (FC) and total fixation duration (TFD) were recorded using Tobii X2-60 eye tracking, physiological arousal using Shimmer3 GSR, and usability using the System Usability Scale. Linear mixed and generalized linear models revealed higher FC (M = 21.922) and GSR (M = 2.213 μS) for traditional materials than for GenAI and multimedia (p < .001; partial η² = .03–.05). TFD did not differ significantly (p = .079). Usability favored multimedia (M = 61.96), followed by GenAI (M = 60.68) and traditional materials (M = 53.52; p = .002; partial η² = .163). GenAI and multimedia showed comparable biometric patterns. Interpretation is limited by five-second slide exposures, one unedited GenAI tool, a single-institution sample, and absent learning-outcome measures.

items.title: Efficient Sensor Configuration for Accelerometer-Based Silent Speech Interfaces: Regionally Distributed Sensor Placement Strategy Considering Articulatory Dynamics
items.abstract: Silent speech interfaces (SSIs) decode articulatory activity without audible speech. Although accelerometer-based SSIs can capture facial and neck movements in compact wearable setups, accelerometer-specific sensor placement has not been systematically examined. This study evaluated all combinations of ten accelerometers across the lower face and neck in a 100 English word silent speech classification task with 20 participants. Subject-dependent classification was performed using a convolutional neural network followed by a bidirectional long short-term memory network. Accuracy improved as the number of sensors increased, reaching a plateau with five sensors. At this point, Sensors 1 and 7, positioned over the upper and lower labial regions, Sensors 4 and 8, located bilaterally along the buccal-mandibular region, and Sensor 5, placed over the left submental region beneath the chin, achieved the highest accuracy of 92.30 ± 4.64% and were selected as the efficient configuration. These five sensors consistently ranked among the most informative locations in standalone performance, perturbation-based explainability, and sensor ablation analyses, indicating that they contributed unique and influential articulatory information. Regional coverage comparisons showed that configurations spanning broader functional articulatory regions outperformed those with more restricted coverage. This placement strategy was further validated using an independent 100-word vocabulary, demonstrating that broad regional coverage remained advantageous despite slight changes in the optimal sensor identities. A practical three-sensor configuration based on this strategy achieved approximately 90% recognition accuracy while substantially reducing hardware complexity. Together, these results support regionally distributed sensor placement as a design strategy for capturing complementary articulatory information in compact accelerometer-based SSI systems.

items.title: ElasticGS: Pose-Aware Dynamic Gaussian Adaptation for Geometry-Consistent Human Digital Twin Reconstruction from Monocular Video
items.abstract: Vision-based 3D sensing provides an effective approach for constructing human-centric digital twins in applications such as ergonomic assessment and human-robot collaboration. However, reconstructing reliable dynamic human digital twins from visual sensor observations remains challenging due to large articulated deformation, which often causes surface discontinuities in existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based human avatars. Although current methods achieve high image-level rendering quality, their Gaussian primitives are not explicitly adapted to pose-induced surface deformation, resulting in cracks and holes during motion. In this work, we propose ElasticGS, a geometry-consistent human digital twin reconstruction framework for vision-based 3D sensing. ElasticGS introduces a training-free Pose-Aware Dynamic Covariance Adaptation strategy, which dynamically adjusts the rotation and anisotropic scale of Gaussian primitives according to local human surface deformation. Specifically, localized Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is performed on deformed SMPL-X mesh neighborhoods to estimate surface stretching directions and magnitudes, enabling Gaussian representations to maintain continuous surface coverage under complex poses. Furthermore, we propose the Avatar Surface Integrity Score (ASIS), a reference-free metric that evaluates structural completeness and surface compactness of reconstructed human avatars without requiring pixel-aligned ground truth. Experiments on the X-Humans, AvatarReX, and People-Snapshot datasets demonstrate that ElasticGS significantly improves surface integrity while maintaining competitive image-level sensing consistency. Compared with ExAvatar, ElasticGS maintains satisfactory rendering quality while improving ASIS from 0.741 to 0.961 on X-Humans, from 0.871 to 0.949 on AvatarReX, and from 0.874 to 0.952 on People-Snapshot. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pose-aware covariance adaptation for robust human digital twin reconstruction in vision-based 3D sensing systems.

items.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

items.title: External Chat or Editor-Integrated? An Empirical Study of AI-Assisted Workflows for Novice Game Development
items.abstract: Vibe coding enables novices to program through conversational intent specification and AI-assisted repair. In game development, generated code must be grounded in scene objects, component settings, and runtime behavior. This study compares two Unity workflows: External Chat, using web-based AI and standalone materials, and Editor-Integrated, embedding AI interaction and materials in the workspace. In a controlled study with 34 undergraduates, both conditions had the same observed self-reported binary completion count, but Editor-Integrated projects showed higher scene-integration scores. Screen-recording coding descriptively indicated more localized repair, project-context use, documentation reference, runtime-evidence prompting, and executable verification in Editor-Integrated, whereas External Chat involved more manual context transfer and whole-code regeneration. Secondary measures showed mixed patterns, including higher descriptive ratings on selected perception item groupings and exploratory, unadjusted follow-up differences in self-reported transfer confidence and continued learning needs. These findings suggest AI-supported programming environments should support system grounding, executable verification, and learner control.

items.title: From Vibe to Code—and Back: Lexical Oscillation in the Formation of Design Intent with Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI design tools make natural-language prompts a starting point for design, placing new articulation demands on designers. Rather than treating prompts as the transmission of preexisting intent, we ask how design intent is formed through situated interaction with AI. Five expert UI/UX designers (11–20 years’ experience, M = 15.4) designed landing-page hero sections with a generative AI tool, recorded through think-aloud and retrospective interviews. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we treated lexical granularity (L1 vibe, L2 design-domain, L3 operational language) as a sensitizing lens. Rather than moving from vibe to code unidirectionally, designers showed lexical oscillation, including returns from operational specificity to ambiguity. Mismatches with AI outputs became occasions to reconsider what they meant, and engagement shifted from instruction to consultation. One non-oscillating trajectory—a negative case—suggested conceptual misalignment as a tentative boundary. We position AI as a non-neutral generative interlocutor and ambiguity as a resource for design judgment.

items.title: Hepatitis B susceptibility, infection and vaccine-induced immunity among health personnel in Sokoto, Nigeria: a cross-sectional serological study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Health personnel in Nigeria have a high occupational risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, and vaccination status is usually established by self-report. The extent to which reported vaccination corresponds to serological protection has not been measured in northern Nigeria. We described HBV infection and immunity among health personnel, compared self-reported vaccination with serological markers and identified factors associated with vaccine-induced immunity, natural immunity and current infection. Methods We conducted an analytical cross-sectional serological study of 473 health personnel selected by multistage sampling from primary, secondary and tertiary facilities in Sokoto State between January and March 2023. An interviewer-administered semi-structured questionnaire was completed, and serum was tested for HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, HBeAg and anti-HBe with a five-panel rapid test. Firth penalised logistic regression was used for each outcome. Results Current infection (HBsAg positive) was found in 7.8% (n = 37; 95% CI: 5.7–10.6) and evidence of any past or current infection in 17.1% (n = 81). Anti-HBs was detected in 16.5% (n = 78): 12.3% (n = 58) had vaccine-induced and 4.2% (n = 20) natural immunity, while 70.6% (n = 334) had no serological marker. Self-reported vaccination had a positive predictive value of 24.3% for vaccine-induced immunity (κ = 0.16). Among 96 participants who reported three or more doses, 69.8% (n = 67) had no detectable anti-HBs and six were HBsAg positive. Vaccine-induced immunity was associated with three or more reported doses (aOR 2.90; 95% CI: 1.37–6.22), positive attitude (aOR 1.98; 95% CI: 1.01–3.90), an employer request for vaccination status (aOR 2.05; 95% CI: 1.03–3.97) and insertion of tubes or catheters (aOR 2.75; 95% CI: 1.08–6.93). Natural immunity was more frequent in primary facilities (aOR 4.84; 95% CI: 1.56–15.30). Current infection was not associated with occupational exposures and was less frequent after more than 10 years of practice (aOR 0.23; 95% CI: 0.06–0.84). Conclusions Most health personnel in Sokoto had no serological protection against HBV, and self-reported vaccination overstated protection. Screening for HBsAg and anti-HBs at recruitment, documented vaccination with post-vaccination testing, and referral of infected staff for care should be part of routine occupational health services.

items.title: Integrated Cognitive Workload and Musculoskeletal Exposure Modeling for Adaptive Ergonomic Work Design
items.abstract: Abstract Cognitive workload, musculoskeletal exposure, fatigue, and limited recovery can jointly affect worker comfort and task performance. However, these factors are often assessed separately, limiting the evaluation of cumulative ergonomic risk over time. This study proposes an integrated ergonomic modeling framework that combines cognitive workload, physical exposure, fatigue accumulation, and recovery within a common assessment structure. Normalized state variables are used to calculate a composite ergonomic risk index, and a proposed multi objective optimization procedure provides a basis for examining alternative task schedules and recovery intervals. Illustrative scenarios compare low, moderate, and high combined demands under specified model assumptions. The proposed analytical design also specifies a procedure for future sensitivity analysis of workload intensity, exposure duration, recovery rate, and worker susceptibility. The illustrative values indicate that higher modeled cognitive workload, physical exposure, and fatigue correspond to greater composite risk under the specified weighting scheme. However, these values are hypothetical and do not represent observed worker data or verified simulation outputs. The framework provides a methodological basis for examining relationships between modeled ergonomic risk and task performance during work schedule planning. Further research should implement reproducible computational experiments, conduct sensitivity analyses, and validate model predictions against measured workload, physical exposure, fatigue, and performance data before practical application.

items.title: Investigating Mechanisms for Ensemble Visualization Interpretation: The Influence of Proximity, Contact, Density, and Spread on Judgments of Risk
items.abstract: Cone of Uncertainty (COU) visualizations are commonly used to convey to the public the uncertain forecast path of an approaching hurricane. However, the cone’s edge causes a precipitous drop in the sense of risk for locations beyond the cone, where no such discontinuity truly exists. An alternative approach using visual ensembles—Animated Risk Trajectories (ARTs)—can overcome this containment effect. However, the mechanism underlying resulting judgments of risk have not been explored. The current study used four different features within ARTs to examine which dimensions contribute to a sense of risk at a target location. Replicating prior findings, ARTs showed a gradual change in judgments of risk with increasing eccentricity from the single most likely storm path, whereas COUs showed a steep decline outside the cone. For ARTs, instances of potential storm paths passing just inside (proximity) or outside (spread) a location did not influence judgments of risk. An instance intersecting a location increased perception of risk (contact), but a larger impact was seen from the presence of a number of instances (density) around the location. Implication of these findings for designing visualizations to elicit a commensurate sense of risk are discussed.

items.title: Perceived Crisis-Management Training Adequacy and Wellbeing Indicators Among Seafarers During the Red Sea Crisis: An Exploratory Survey
items.abstract: Global shipping carries over 80% of world trade, yet existing supply-chain-resilience theory models resilience at the level of the firm, node and network, without treating the workforce operating those nodes as a variable. This exploratory study addresses that gap using the 2023–2026 Red Sea/Houthi crisis as its empirical setting. A pilot-scale, cross-sectional online survey of 64 serving seafarers combined closed-ended items with qualitative content analysis of two open-text questions. Seafarers who had witnessed or been directly involved in a security incident rated STCW crisis-management training as less adequate for conflict-area risk than those without such exposure (Mann–Whitney U = 227.0, p = 0.007, r = 0.34), the only comparison that remained significant after Holm adjustment within its family of tests; Red Sea transit or Cape of Good Hope rerouting without an incident was not associated with lower ratings. Open-text responses identified situational information and realistic scenario-based drills, rather than generic compliance training, as the specific gap, and a minority questioned seafarers’ right to decline a high-risk voyage. Because fatigue and psychological distress could be captured only through single, non-validated items, findings on these outcomes are indicative only. Building on these results, the study proposes, as exploratory propositions for future testing rather than established relationships, two human-factor pathways through which geopolitical risk may affect operational resilience: a training-competence pathway and a retention/psychological-contract pathway. The study contributes hypothesis-generating evidence, gathered directly from an affected workforce, and derives practical and policy recommendations for STCW training content and seafarer consent protections.

items.title: Prevalence and Environmental Correlates of Back Pain among Schoolchildren in Maiduguri Metropolis, North-Eastern Nigeria: A Cross-Sectional Multi-Stage Survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background Low back pain (LBP) among adolescents represents a significant but understudied public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa. This study investigated the prevalence and multi-factorial determinants of LBP among secondary school students in Maiduguri Metropolis, North-Eastern Nigeria. Methods Using a multi-stage stratified sampling technique, this cross-sectional survey recruited 1,012 adolescents from both public and private schools. Participant demographics, commuting characteristics, carrying habits, and spinal pain histories were assessed via a validated questionnaire. Objective measurements of standing height, body mass, and absolute backpack weight were taken using calibrated equipment to determine relative load percentage (% body weight [%BW]). Statistical analyses included Spearman rank correlations and multivariable binary logistic regression to evaluate independent risk factors (aOR, 95 CI). Results Among analyzed respondents (N = 1,005), overall LBP prevalence was 55.6% (n = 559), with within-sex rates of 58.4% for males (272/466) and 53.2% for females (287/539). Unadjusted correlation analysis showed mild positive associations between pain severity and both absolute bag weight (r s = + 0.120, p < 0.001) and relative bag load (r s = + 0.103, p = 0.001). However, after multivariable adjustments (chi 2 = 28.44, p < 0.001), carrying loads > 10% BW failed to maintain independent statistical significance (aOR = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.91–1.61, p = 0.188). The principal independent determinants of LBP were female sex (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.08–1.87, p = 0.012), overweight/obese BMI (aOR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.10–2.16, p = 0.011), and daily carriage times exceeding 30 minutes (aOR = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.09–1.93, p = 0.010). Conclusion Spinal discomfort is widespread among Nigerian secondary school students and driven by complex interactions. Isolated schoolbag weight is a weaker predictor of pain than physical exposure duration (> 30mins/day) and personal attributes (sex and BMI). Preventative school ergonomics should prioritize active transit planning and physical wellness over strict weight limits alone.

items.title: Process evaluation of a migrant-inclusive risk communication and community engagement intervention: lessons from the Health Handbook for Vietnamese Workers in Japan
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Migrant workers in Japan face persistent barriers in accessing timely and culturally appropriate health information owing to language constraints, complex administrative systems, and fragmented risk communication channels. These challenges have been exacerbated during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the need for migrant-inclusive risk communication and community engagement (RCCE). In response, the Government of Vietnam, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), and Japanese partners collaboratively developed the Health Handbook for Vietnamese Workers in Japan as a transnational RCCE intervention. METHODS: This study evaluates a process the development, dissemination, monitoring, and iterative adaptation of the Handbook. Multiple data sources were triangulated, including mixed-methods situation analyses, technical working group documentation, Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) assessment, digital analytics, and qualitative stakeholder feedback. Qualitative data were analysed using an inductive thematic approach. Themes generated from the data were subsequently interpreted in relation to RCCE principles and the social determinants of health framework to identify mechanisms relevant to the implementation of a migrant-inclusive RCCE. RESULTS: The evaluation identified three interrelated mechanisms that appeared to support migrant-inclusive RCCE: (1) addressing structural vulnerabilities; (2) deploying multichannel communication strategies tailored to migrants; and (3) engaging migrant communities and stakeholders. The Handbook was designed to provide practical health information, particularly on occupational health, healthcare navigation, and rights-related topics. Digital analytics showed an increased reach following collaboration with community-based platforms, while the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) assessment indicated high understandability (81.3%) but moderate actionability (66.7%), indicating a need for iterative revisions. The intervention provided a platform for multi-sectoral collaboration and supported the continuity of health messaging across the migration cycle. CONCLUSIONS: This study illustrates that migrant-inclusive RCCE, when implemented through participatory, multi-sectoral, and transnational approaches, may support more equitable access to health information and contribute to health system resilience. Integrating such approaches within national preparedness frameworks may strengthen effective emergency responses and help address the structural determinants that shape migrant health by influencing exposure to health risks, access to reliable information and essential services, and the ability to seek timely and appropriate care.

items.title: Recent Developments in Global Probabilistic Turbulence Forecast Products for Aeronautical Meteorology at Deutscher Wetterdienst
items.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence is a major hazard for commercial flight operations. As a result, reliable and easily interpretable meteorological forecast data for this hazard is paramount to the safety of aircraft, crew and passengers. To meet this requirement, Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD) has further improved their forecast products by blending the traditional deterministic numerical weather prediction of the Eddy Dissipation Parameter (EDP) with the probabilistic forecast to exceed the severe turbulence threshold of the EDP from its operational ensemble prediction system (EPS). Building on those results and inspired by an agile co-design approach with key users, a turbulence advisory was conceived which condenses three-dimensional spatial information into two dimensions in order to further support situational awareness and complement traditional aeronautical meteorological charts. In this technical paper, the necessity for products of this kind is motivated and their design and specifications are briefly explained.
